title: Rules Rail
context: Grade 4, and the chapter stops working here to ask what subtraction will and will not allow. An adult sees four shortcuts and a box about order. What is actually at stake is a rule carried over from the chapter before. There, two numbers being added could be swapped freely and the answer did not care. Here they cannot, and a child who assumes otherwise writes the smaller number on top and then takes the bigger digit from the smaller one column by column, which is the tidiest way there is of getting every column wrong.

writeup.why: Find out which things you are allowed to do to a subtraction, and the one thing that addition allows and this does not.
writeup.look: A rail with a number card riding on it, rule cards waiting underneath, and a two lane order gate standing at its left hand end.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rules Rail' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the rule cards run against the rule cards this phase has laid out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each card leaves the rail and the second fixed at the number of cards waiting. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The order gate stands at the left of the working area, 300 by 300 at 64,202: two lanes 300 by 138 one above the other, each with a mouth at its left, a throat, and an opening at its right where an answer comes out. The same pair of numbers is loaded into both lanes, the greater one leading in the upper lane and the smaller one leading in the lower, and both lanes run together on one press. The upper lane carries its pair through and sets an answer down at its opening; the lower lane runs in step until it reaches a column with less in it than is being asked for, and there it simply stops, with the pair left standing in the throat, nothing marked and no red anywhere. The swap control sits under the gate at 64,516, 300 by 76: pressed while a jam is still showing, it loads the identical pair into both lanes as an addition instead, both lanes run to the end, and the two totals land at their openings on the same tick, so the rule that holds and the rule that does not are read side by side without either being announced. The rail runs across the rest of the working area, 720 by 8 at 394,320, carrying one number card 300 by 104 that rides along it. The place chart slides in behind the number, 720 by 150 at 394,232, one named place above each digit and read out from the right hand end. The six rule cards lie beneath the rail in two rows of three, each 168 by 84 with 12 between them, the upper row at 394,400 reading take nothing, take one and take the number itself, the lower row at 394,496 reading take ten, take a hundred and take a thousand. A card dragged on to the rail acts in one movement while the place it names lights in the chart, and hold the rest draws every other digit pinned in place for as long as the movement lasts. Take one steps the whole card back to the number just before it, with the rollover drawn at the digit where it happens; take nothing moves nothing at all and the card is read out afterwards as the same number it arrived as; take the number itself empties the card and leaves it standing blank. The fact bay runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 120 at 64,586, holding three number cards and three lines: the addition fact along the top and two empty subtraction lines under it, both of which have to begin from the total card. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever an answer is asked for, and beside them a word pad carrying the five terms the chapter closes on, minuend, subtrahend, difference, rounding and estimate, turned towards a partner for the quiz and answered by press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the greater number standing on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, the answer under the rule is green, the ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a column that has lent is told by the single strike through its digit and by the smaller value written small above it. No lane of the order gate is ever marked wrong and no jam is ever drawn in red: a lane that stops has simply run out of things to take, and that is a fact about the numbers rather than a mistake the child made.
writeup.finish: The card shows the rail with the last rule that ran still lit, and the order gate holding the pair that jammed.

phases.win: one lane jams for want of enough to take, and both addition lanes land together
phases.does: runs both lanes, watches one jam, then loads the pair as an addition
phases.goal: the greater number has to go first, unlike two numbers being added
phases.says: Swap them over. Does subtraction let you? Did adding let you?
phases.check: In an addition you may write the two numbers in either order. Write down what happens if you try that in a subtraction.
phases.feels: one of the two lanes simply has nothing left in it to take from
phases.hands: On squared paper write eighteen take ten and work it. Then write ten take eighteen underneath and try to work it column by column out loud, without being rescued. Then write the same two numbers as an addition, once each way round, and put the two totals side by side. Ask which of the two workings let the numbers be swapped and which one did not.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers is leading in the lane that stopped? Second rung, the phase's: can more be taken out of a number than the number holds? Third rung: the gate is cut to a single column pair and the child sends it through both ways. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the chapter before this one taught that two numbers being added may be written in either order and the total does not change, and nothing in the way a subtraction is written says the rule has stopped.
wrong.move: swaps the two numbers over so that the subtraction reads the easier way round, because addition allowed exactly that.
wrong.screen: the swapped pair is sent through the gate as it stands and the lane jams at the first column with less in it than is being asked for, with the pair left standing and nothing marked. The swap control then loads the identical two numbers as an addition, both lanes run to the end and their totals land together, and the two runs are left on the stage one above the other so that the rule that holds and the rule that does not can be read side by side.

wrong.why: a column turned round quietly gives an answer where there was not one to be had, and a lane that reaches its opening looks like a lane that worked.
wrong.move: keeps the smaller number in front and takes the smaller digit from the greater one in each column, so that the lane runs after all.
wrong.screen: the lane is run again at walking pace with each column read out in the order it is written, the leading number's digit named first, and every column the child turned round is ringed amber and read again as it stands. The same pair is then run the proper way round in the lane above, and the two answers stand at their openings together with the check by addition run on each of them.

phases.screen: the order gate with the same pair loaded into both of its lanes
phases.soWhat: The greater number goes first in a subtraction and the two cannot be swapped, though the two numbers in an addition can.

phases.win: the card stands unchanged, steps back one, and empties, in that order
phases.does: drops each of the three in turn and says what moved before it moves
phases.goal: three rules that need no columns at all
phases.says: Take nothing. Take one. Take the whole thing. Say each answer before you drop it.
phases.check: Away from the screen: what is left when a number has nothing taken from it, and what is left when it has the whole of itself taken from it?
phases.feels: three answers, and not one column worked between them
phases.hands: Write 62,904 three times down a sheet of squared paper and take nothing from the first, one from the second and the whole number from the third. Insist that each answer is said out loud before it is written, and that nothing is set out in columns. Then ask which of the three answers would change if the number had been six digits long instead.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how much was actually taken off the card? Second rung, the phase's: if nothing left the card, what can be standing on it? Third rung: the rail is cut to a two digit number and all three cards are run on it in turn. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: taking nothing away and taking the whole number away are met one after the other, and the word nothing turns up in both of them.
wrong.move: writes nothing at all as the answer when nothing has been taken away, because the two rules were learnt in the same breath.
wrong.screen: the nothing card runs again at walking pace with the place chart behind the number and every digit pinned, and not one of them moves; the card that leaves the rail is read out place by place as the same number it arrived as. The itself card is then run on a second card beside it and that one empties, and the two cards are left standing together for comparison.

wrong.why: one more and one less are the same small step in opposite directions, and the number that comes next is the one said aloud far more often.
wrong.move: steps the card forward to the number just after instead of back to the number just before.
wrong.screen: a short strip of the numbers either side of the card is drawn under the rail with the card sitting on its own place, and the step is animated along it; the number just before lights and the number just after is left plain. The child's answer stays on the strip exactly where it was put, one place past the card, and both stay showing.

phases.screen: a number on the rail with the nothing, one and itself cards waiting
phases.soWhat: Taking nothing leaves a number alone, taking one steps it back to the number just before it, and taking a number from itself empties it.
phases.concept: One, nothing, and the number itself

phases.win: the named digit drops by one, the rest stay pinned and the chart agrees
phases.does: names the digit that will drop, then drops the card and checks
phases.goal: a round amount drops the digit of its own place and no other
phases.says: Which digit is going to move this time? Say it before you drop the card.
phases.check: Take a thousand away from a six digit number of your own. Which digit changed, and how did you find it?
phases.feels: one digit moves and none of the others cares
phases.hands: Write 58,271 on squared paper and take ten from it, then a hundred, then a thousand, each from the original number. Ring the digit that changed each time and check that every other digit was copied down untouched. Then do the same three on 4,37,912 and ask whether the ringed digit sits in the same position along the number as it did before.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which place does this card name? Second rung, the phase's: which end of the number do you count the places from? Third rung: the chart is cut to three places with a three digit number on the rail and the child runs the ten card and the hundred card on it. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a number is read from the left, and on a five digit number counting from either end can land on the same digit, which is often enough for the habit to survive unnoticed.
wrong.move: counts the places from the left hand end of the number, so the digit that drops is the wrong one.
wrong.screen: the place chart slides in behind the number and is read out from the right hand end, with the place the card names lit the whole way. The digit the child dropped keeps its own mark where it was put, and the same rule card is then run on 4,37,912, where 4,36,912 and 4,27,912 stand one under the other and the two ways of counting plainly part.

wrong.why: every change to a number so far has meant a column being worked and something moving next door, and a digit standing perfectly still while its neighbour drops looks unfinished.
wrong.move: drops the named digit and nudges the digits beside it as well, as though the whole number had to shift along.
wrong.screen: hold the rest pins every other digit and the card is run again with each pinned digit drawn holding its place as the movement passes it. The number is then read out place by place before and after, the two readings standing one under the other, and only the single named place differs between them.

phases.screen: the rail with the place chart behind the number and every digit pinned
phases.soWhat: Taking ten drops the tens digit, taking a hundred drops the hundreds digit and taking a thousand drops the thousands digit, and nothing else moves.
phases.concept: Ten, a hundred and a thousand each touch one digit

phases.win: both subtraction facts stand under the addition, built from the same three cards
phases.does: turns the fact over and writes both subtraction facts from the same cards
phases.goal: one addition fact turns over into two subtraction facts
phases.says: Three cards, and you have written one fact. How many more are hiding in them?
phases.check: You are given two numbers and the total they make. How many subtraction facts can you write from them, and which number does each one begin at?
phases.feels: three cards, and every one of the three facts uses all three of them
phases.hands: Write 32,140 + 45,209 = 77,349 on a strip of paper and cut the strip into three number cards. Ask for every true line that can be made from those three cards and no others, and have each one written out. Then ask which card every subtraction line had to begin from, and why that is so.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the three cards is the total? Second rung, the phase's: if one part is taken off the total, which card is left? Third rung: the bay is cut to a two digit addition fact and the child writes both subtraction lines from it. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the three cards can be laid out in more ways than three, and a subtraction using two of them looks like it belongs to the same family as the others.
wrong.move: writes a subtraction that takes one of the two parts away from the other part.
wrong.screen: the three cards are read again as two parts and a total with the total card lit, and the child's line is worked anyway in the lane beside it, landing on 13,069, which is not written on any of the three cards. Both lines stay on the stage, with the lines that begin from the total lit and the one that does not left plain.

wrong.why: turning the addition over once has already produced something new, and one new fact feels like a complete answer to the question that was asked.
wrong.move: writes one subtraction fact and reports the fact bay finished.
wrong.screen: the fact bay keeps the line the child wrote and lifts the part card that line took away, leaving the other part standing on its own and unused; the bay then asks for a line that begins at the total and ends on that card, and both subtraction facts finish standing under the addition, all three built from the same three cards.

phases.screen: the fact bay holding one addition fact on three cards
phases.soWhat: Two numbers and their total hold one addition fact and two subtraction facts.
phases.concept: Every addition fact holds two subtraction facts

writeup.delight: The first phase, at the order gate. The same pair is sent into both lanes on one press and they run in step, column for column, until the lower lane arrives at a column with less in it than is being asked for and simply comes to a halt, with the pair still standing in the throat and nothing marked anywhere. Press the swap control while that jam is still sitting on the stage and the identical two numbers are loaded as an addition: both lanes run all the way through this time, and their two totals land at the openings on the very same tick. The jam and the pair of matching totals are left on the stage together, and the voice says nothing about either.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the order gate stands at the left with the same pair of numbers already loaded into both of its lanes, the greater one leading in the upper lane and the smaller one leading in the lower, and both mouths closed. On the second a number card rides the middle of the rail with three rule cards waiting under it, one reading take nothing, one take one and one take the number itself. On the third the place chart has already slid in behind the number and every digit is pinned, with the three round amount cards lying below. On the fourth the fact bay holds one addition fact on three cards and two empty lines beneath it. The running count at the top left holds the rule cards run against the rule cards waiting, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the closed mouth of the lower lane, or the nothing card, or the digit the next card will act on, or the total card in the fact bay, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what is going to happen before anything is dropped. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number on the rail, any rule card, with the order gate open and the fact bay loaded alongside. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on order, on nothing and one and the number itself, on which digit a round amount touches, and on turning an addition fact over.
voiceLines: A number rides the rail. Say what a rule card will do to it before you drop the card.
Swap them over. Does subtraction let you? Did adding let you?
Take nothing. Take one. Take the whole thing. Say each answer before you drop it.
Which digit is going to move this time? Say it before you drop the card.
Three cards, and you have written one fact. How many more are hiding in them?
Another number on the rail. Which digit is going to move this time?
Free play. Any number, any rule card, the order gate open and the fact bay loaded.
Send that card again at walking pace and watch the place chart behind the number.
Every rule run without a column being worked, and one thing subtraction would not let you do.

observations.why: The lane led by the smaller number reaches a column with less in it than is being asked for.
observations.soWhat: The two numbers in a subtraction cannot be swapped, and the greater one has to go first.
observations.observe: The same pair ran into both lanes together and only one of the two lanes came out with an answer.

observations.why: Adding puts two amounts together, and it makes no difference which of them is counted on to the other.
observations.soWhat: The order rule from the chapter before is still true; it is simply not this chapter's rule.
observations.observe: Loaded as an addition, that very same pair ran in both lanes and the two totals landed together.

observations.why: Ten, a hundred and a thousand are each worth exactly one of the place they name.
observations.soWhat: A round amount is taken off a number by sight, without anything being set out in columns.
observations.observe: Taking a round amount moved one digit and left every other digit standing exactly where it was.

observations.why: Two parts and a total are one relationship, and it can be written from the total as well as towards it.
observations.soWhat: Knowing an addition fact is already knowing two subtraction facts.
observations.observe: Three number cards produced three facts, and two of the three were subtractions.

serves.exercise: filling in the blanks where zero, one, ten, a hundred or a thousand is taken away
writing two subtraction facts for each of the four given addition facts
solving the given lines that add and take away in one working
subtracting the sum of the two given numbers from the greatest six digit number
subtracting each given pair and checking the answer by a suitable addition
quizzing a partner on the five vocabulary terms of the chapter

source_tool.description: A rail runs across the stage with a number card riding on it and a row of rule cards waiting underneath: take nothing, take one, take the number itself, take ten, take a hundred, take a thousand. A rule card dropped onto the rail acts on the number in one movement and a place chart slides in behind it, so the digit that moved is named as it moves and every other digit is pinned visibly still. Taking one steps the whole card back to the number just before it. Taking nothing moves nothing at all. Taking the number itself empties the card. At the left of the rail stands an order gate with two lanes. The same pair of numbers runs through both lanes at once, the greater number first in one lane and the smaller number first in the other, and the second lane jams: there is not that much there to take away. A swap control sitting beside it loads the same pair into an addition, where both lanes run and their answers land together, so the two rules can be read against each other without either being stated. A fact bay below holds one addition fact on three cards and turns it over into the two subtraction facts hiding inside it. A word pad carries the five terms of the chapter for a partner to be quizzed on.
source_tool.art_direction: A number card on a rail, rule cards below / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that untie themselves, a rule between the number taken away and the answer, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A subtraction is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the greater number on top, the two numbers aligned by their right ends, the minus sign to the left of the lower row, and a horizontal rule between that row and the answer. A bare line of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach taking away.

A trade is always drawn as both of its halves. The lending column keeps its digit, struck through once, with its new and smaller value written small above it, and the ten it lent is drawn arriving in the column on its right. A short arrow runs from the lending column to the receiving one, left to right, never the other way.

A check by addition is drawn under the subtraction it tests, and the total it comes to is set beside the number the working started from, so the two can be read against each other without anything being cleared.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The greater number on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, and the answer under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, and a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, so the two halves of one trade are told apart at a glance. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a lending column is told apart by the strike through its digit and by the smaller digit written above it before it is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Send that card again at walking pace and watch the place chart behind the number.
voice.onNext: Another number on the rail. Which digit is going to move this time?
voice.opening: A number rides the rail. Say what a rule card will do to it before you drop the card.
voice.onFinish: Every rule run without a column being worked, and one thing subtraction would not let you do.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any number, any rule card, the order gate open and the fact bay loaded.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: One, nothing, and the number itself
Ten, a hundred and a thousand each touch one digit
Every addition fact holds two subtraction facts

placement.where: After the order box has been read aloud and before any of the rules are named. The tool is what runs the same pair both ways at once, which a written line can only do by being worked twice and compared afterwards.

answer_key.rule: The two numbers in a subtraction cannot be swapped: the greater one has to go first, and that is not a choice. Two numbers being added may be swapped freely, which is the rule this one is easily mistaken for. Taking one away gives the number just before it, its predecessor. Taking nothing away leaves a number exactly as it was. Taking a number away from itself leaves nothing. Taking ten drops the tens digit by one, taking a hundred drops the hundreds digit and taking a thousand drops the thousands digit, with every other digit standing still. Every addition fact holds two subtraction facts, one for each number that was added.
answer_key.wrong: The rule card slides back off the rail and runs again at walking pace, with the place chart behind the number and the digit that should move named before it moves. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Working 61 - 24 gives 37, because the ones fetch a ten from the tens on their left.
Swapping them asks for 61 to be taken from 24, and there is not that much there to take.
So the two numbers in a subtraction cannot be swapped, though two numbers being added can.
items.answer: No. 61 - 24 = 37, but 61 cannot be taken from 24 at all
items.question: Take 24 from 61. Now try taking 61 from 24. Is it the same answer?
items.checkpoint: Adding lets its two numbers swap places. Subtraction does not.
items.misconception: Carrying the swapping rule over from addition and writing the smaller number on top.

steps: Taking nothing away puts nothing into any column, so 45,208 - 0 = 45,208.
Taking one away gives the number just before it, so 45,208 - 1 = 45,207.
Taking a number away from itself leaves nothing at all, so 45,208 - 45,208 = 0.
items.question: Write the answers to 45,208 - 0, then 45,208 - 1, then 45,208 - 45,208.
items.checkpoint: Nothing leaves a number alone, one steps it back, and itself empties it.
items.misconception: Writing 0 for 45,208 - 0, by reading the rule for taking a number from itself.

steps: Taking a hundred drops the digit in the hundreds place, which is 5, so it becomes 4.
That gives 74,436, with every other digit standing exactly where it was.
Taking a thousand drops the thousands digit from 4 to 3 instead, which gives 73,536.
items.answer: 74,436 and 73,536. The hundreds digit dropped first, then the thousands digit
items.question: Take 100 from 74,536, then take 1000 from 74,536, and say which digit moved each time.
items.checkpoint: A round amount drops the digit of its own place, whatever the number looks like.
items.misconception: Counting places from the left hand end of the number instead of the right.

steps: The total is 67,353, and the two numbers that made it are 41,203 and 26,150.
Take the first of them away from the total and the second one is left.
Take the second away instead and the first is left, which gives the two facts.
items.question: From the addition fact 41,203 + 26,150 = 67,353, write the two subtraction facts.
items.checkpoint: Two numbers and their total make one addition fact and two subtraction facts.
items.misconception: Writing 41,203 - 26,150 as a subtraction fact, which takes one part from another part.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Does 92,415 - 30,207 give the same answer as 30,207 - 92,415?
items.final_answer: No. The first gives 62,208, and the second cannot be worked, because the greater number has to go first

items.question: In addition you may swap the two numbers over. What is the rule in subtraction?
items.final_answer: The two numbers cannot be swapped, and the greater one goes first

items.question: A child takes 1000 from 83,472 and writes 83,372. Is that right?
items.final_answer: No. It should be 82,472, because taking a thousand drops the thousands digit and not the hundreds digit

items.question: From 35,124 + 42,613 = 77,737, write the two subtraction facts.
Subtract the sum of 24,180 and 31,725 from 99,999.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: carries one number card across the stage for the rules to act on
takes nothing, one, the number itself, ten, a hundred or a thousand
names the place of the digit that moved, behind the number
pins every other digit visibly still while one drops
runs the same pair with the greater number first and with the smaller first
loads the same pair as an addition, where both lanes run
turns one addition fact over into the two subtraction facts inside it
holds the chapter terms for a partner to be quizzed on

teaching_notes: Start at the order gate and start it as a question, not as a rule. The chapter before this one taught that two numbers being added may be swapped over and nothing changes, so every child in the room arrives expecting the same here, and telling them otherwise is much weaker than letting the second lane jam in front of them. Run the same pair as an addition straight afterwards, while the jam is still on the stage, so the two rules are held apart by having been seen side by side. For the rules that need no columns, make them say the answer before the card drops every single time, because a rule used after the fact is only a check and a rule used before it is a rule. Watch for the child who counts places from the left hand end: with a five digit number they will be right often enough to keep doing it, and a six digit number then catches them out. The fact bay is worth ending on. Three cards, one addition and two subtractions, and the two subtractions both take a part from the total rather than a part from a part. The vocabulary quiz works best with the word pad turned towards a partner and the five terms asked in a different order each time.
generation_prompt: Build a rules tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A horizontal rail carries a single number card, with a row of rule cards beneath it reading take nothing, take one, take the number itself, take ten, take a hundred and take a thousand. Dragging a rule card onto the rail acts on the number in one animated movement while a place value chart slides in behind the number naming the place that changed, and a hold the rest control pins every other digit visibly still. Taking one steps the card back to its predecessor with the rollover drawn where it happens; taking nothing moves nothing; taking the number itself empties the card. At the left hand end stands an order gate with two lanes, running the same pair of numbers with the greater first in one lane and the smaller first in the other; the second lane visibly jams for want of enough to take away, and nothing is marked wrong. A swap control loads the same pair as an addition instead, where both lanes run to completion and their totals land together for comparison. A fact bay below holds one addition fact on three number cards and turns it over into the two subtraction facts built from the same three cards. A word pad at the side holds the chapter terms for a partner quiz. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put a number on the rail and drop a rule card onto it. Say which digit will move before it moves. Then send a pair through the order gate both ways round and see which lane jams. Finish at the fact bay and write both subtraction facts from one addition.
